checkpoints.title: The Windows partition
checkpoints.question: In 512-byte sectors, at which sector does the partition that contains Windows start?
hints: The image's partition table is read with `mmls`.
Two partitions are NTFS. The small first one only holds boot files. Windows is on the large one.
Run `mmls` on the E01 file and read the Start column for the large NTFS partition.
checkpoints.success: Correct. Every Sleuth Kit command on this image needs that offset. Picking the first NTFS partition is the classic mistake.

checkpoints.title: Do the logs match the image?
checkpoints.question: Compute the SHA-256 of `Security.evtx` inside the mounted image. What are its last 8 characters?
hints: Windows keeps its event logs in `Windows/System32/winevt/Logs` on the mounted image.
Use `sha256sum` on `Security.evtx` there.
Compare the result with the line for `evidence/DC01/evtx/Security.evtx` in `/cases/szechuan/MANIFEST.sha256`. The answer is the last 8 characters.
checkpoints.success: Correct, and it equals the hash in the log kit's manifest. You have shown that the logs you were given came from the image you verified.

checkpoints.title: The failed logons
checkpoints.question: How many Security 4625 (failed logon) records on DC01 have a WorkstationName of exactly `kali`?
hints: Failed logons are event 4625 in the Security log. The CSV is `derived/DC01/DC01-evtxecmd.csv`.
Look at the WorkstationName field of those records. Then look at what their IpAddress field contains.
Count the rows where the event ID is 4625, the channel is Security, and WorkstationName is `kali`.
checkpoints.success: Correct. Notice that these records have no source address at all. Anyone who says "95 failures from 194.61.24.102 in the Security log" has not opened the records.

checkpoints.title: The first way in
checkpoints.question: Among DC01 Security 4624 records with IpAddress 194.61.24.102 and LogonType 10, what is the TargetLogonId of the earliest one?
hints: Successful logons are Security event 4624. A Remote Desktop logon has LogonType 10.
Keep only the records whose IpAddress is 194.61.24.102 and whose LogonType is 10, and sort them by time.
The answer is the TargetLogonId of the earliest one. It looks like `0x` followed by six characters.
checkpoints.success: Correct: record 7495. A logon ID names one session, and every later event from that session carries it.

checkpoints.title: The session that moved on
checkpoints.question: DC01 Security 4648 records that target the server DESKTOP-SDN1RPT: what is their SubjectLogonId?
hints: Event 4648 means someone used explicit credentials to reach another machine. It is logged on the machine they were sitting at.
Find the DC01 Security 4648 records whose TargetServerName is DESKTOP-SDN1RPT.
The answer is their SubjectLogonId. Compare it with your answer to checkpoint 4.
checkpoints.success: Correct. It is not the session from checkpoint 4. The attacker logged on several times, and this later session is the one that reached the desktop.

checkpoints.title: The implant's file record
checkpoints.question: What is the file-table (MFT) record number of `Windows\System32\coreupdater.exe` in the image?
hints: Every file on NTFS has a numbered record in the master file table.
Sleuth Kit's `ifind -n <path>` gives the record number for a path. It needs the partition offset from checkpoint 1.
Run `ifind` with `-o 718848` and `-n /Windows/System32/coreupdater.exe` on the E01 file.
checkpoints.success: Correct. That number is how you cite this file. Check the name carefully: it ends in "r".

checkpoints.title: Moved or copied?
checkpoints.question: In the NTFS change journal, what is the USN of the record that renamed `coreupdater.exe` into the System32 folder?
hints: NTFS logs file changes in a journal at `$Extend/$UsnJrnl:$J`. MFTECmd turns it into a CSV.
Filter the journal for the name `coreupdater.exe` and look for records whose reason includes RenameNewName. Look at their parent folder.
There are two such renames. You want the one whose parent is the System32 folder, not Downloads. The answer is its update sequence number.
checkpoints.success: Correct. The file kept the same record number, 87137, before and after. It was moved from Downloads, not copied.

checkpoints.title: The service
checkpoints.question: What is the EventRecordID of the DC01 System 7045 event that installed the service named `coreupdater`?
hints: Windows writes System event 7045 when a new service is installed.
Filter the DC01 CSV for event ID 7045 in the System channel and the service name `coreupdater`.
The answer is the record number of that event, not the event ID.
checkpoints.success: Correct. Now compare this event's time with the last-write time of the service's registry key in the image. They are identical, which ties the log to the disk.

checkpoints.title: Did it run?
checkpoints.question: What run count does the Administrator's UserAssist record show for `coreupdater.exe`?
hints: UserAssist lives in a user's `NTUSER.DAT` registry hive and counts programs started through the desktop.
Run RegRipper's `userassist` plugin on the Administrator's `NTUSER.DAT` in the mounted image.
Find the line for `coreupdater.exe`. The run count is the number in parentheses.
checkpoints.success: Correct. This is thin evidence: this server has no Prefetch, and the implant is missing from the other usual execution records. Say what the record shows, not more.

checkpoints.title: The Recycle Bin
checkpoints.question: What is the name of the Recycle Bin index file (the `$I` file) on the image? Include the `$` and the extension.
hints: The Recycle Bin is the hidden folder `$Recycle.Bin` at the top of the volume, with one subfolder per user.
Each deleted item is a pair: a `$I` file holding the original path, size, and deletion time, and a `$R` file holding the content.
List the contents of the subfolders of `$Recycle.Bin` on the mounted image. RBCmd decodes the `$I` file.
checkpoints.success: Correct. Decode it: it tells you which file was deleted, from where, and when.

checkpoints.title: The changed timestamps
checkpoints.question: For `Beth_Secret.txt`, how many seconds passed between the journal record that created it and the later journal record that changed its basic information? Round down to a whole number.
hints: Use the change journal CSV from checkpoint 7 and filter for `Beth_Secret.txt`. Note its EntryNumber and SequenceNumber.

List every journal record with that EntryNumber and SequenceNumber, whatever its name. Find the FileCreate record, and the later record whose reason is BasicInfoChange. That reason covers timestamp changes.
Subtract the first time from the second, in seconds, and round down.
checkpoints.success: Correct. Now compare the file's two sets of timestamps in its MFT record. One set was changed after the fact and the other was not.

checkpoints.title: The clock
checkpoints.question: Using the network sensor summary and the logs, how many hours ahead of the sensor is the machines' clock? Round to the nearest whole hour.
hints: `derived/NETWORK/rdp-sensor-summary.txt` gives times from the network sensor, whose clock is correct.
Find one event that both sources recorded, for example the single Remote Desktop connection from 10.42.85.10 to 10.42.85.115.
Subtract the sensor's time from the log's time for that event and round to the nearest hour.
checkpoints.success: Correct. Every time on this server, in the logs and on the disk, is one hour ahead. Correct your timeline before you compare it with anything else.
